\chapter{Today, Yesterday, and the Year}
\label{ch:ta-today-yesterday-and-the-year}
\hlchaptermodality{73}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say today, yesterday and before in Tamil, and name a month and a year.}

Complete TA-C73-year and say all five words of the chapter in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[iṉṟu]{\ta{இன்று} (iṉṟu) — today}

\label{lesson:TA-C73-today}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{aḻu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{இன்று}}
\textbf{\ta{இன்று}} (\emph{iṉṟu}) — \textquotedblleft{}today\textquotedblright{}.

\textquotedblleft{}Today\textquotedblright{}.

You already have \ta{நாள்} (\emph{nāḷ}), the day itself, and \ta{நாளை} (\emph{nāḷai}), tomorrow. \ta{இன்று} is the day you are standing in, and it completes the middle of that little set.

This is the careful, written form, and it is the one printed on a page. In fast speech you will also hear \ta{இன்னைக்கு} (\emph{iṉṉaikku}) for the same thing — worth recognising, but \ta{இன்று} is the one to say.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The day you are standing in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{iṉṟu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nāḷ}, then \emph{iṉṟu}, then \emph{nāḷai}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{siri}, then say \emph{aḻu}, then say \emph{iṉṟu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{இன்று} mean, and which word already gave you \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}? (\textquotedblleft{}Today\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{\ta{நாளை}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nēṟṟu]{\ta{நேற்று} (nēṟṟu) — yesterday}

\label{lesson:TA-C73-yesterday}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{iṉṟu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நேற்று}}
\textbf{\ta{நேற்று}} (\emph{nēṟṟu}) — \textquotedblleft{}yesterday\textquotedblright{}.

\textquotedblleft{}Yesterday\textquotedblright{} — the third corner of the same triangle: \ta{நேற்று}, \ta{இன்று}, \ta{நாளை}.

The middle is a doubled \textbf{\ta{ற்ற}}, the hard r held long, and it is the sound that most often catches a new speaker out. Say it slowly: the first \ta{ற} has a \ta{புள்ளி} and no vowel, so it leans straight onto the second.

With three words you can now place any day against the one you are in.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and the days on either side of today are named.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nēṟṟu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nēṟṟu}, \emph{iṉṟu}, \emph{nāḷai} — the three, in order
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nēṟṟu} once more, holding the doubled \ta{ற}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{aḻu}, then say \emph{iṉṟu}, then say \emph{nēṟṟu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the three days in order, starting with yesterday. (\textbf{\ta{நேற்று}, \ta{இன்று}, \ta{நாளை}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[iṉṟu]{\ta{இன்று} — a word that opens on a vowel}

\label{lesson:TA-W28-read-inru}



\begin{quote}
Before the page: you can say \emph{iṉṟu} and \emph{nēṟṟu}. Now read the first one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{இன்று} — a word that opens on a vowel}
\textbf{\ta{இன்று}} puts together two things you have read separately: a word that \textbf{begins} with an independent vowel, and a \ta{புள்ளி} making one consonant lean on the next.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{இ}} & \emph{i} & the free-standing letter, because the word opens on the vowel \\
\textbf{\ta{ன்}} & \emph{ṉ} & \ta{ன} with a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}} — no vowel of its own \\
\textbf{\ta{று}} & \emph{ṟu} & \ta{ற} with the \textbf{\ta{ு}} sign \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{இ} · \ta{ன்} · \ta{று} $\to$ \ta{இன்று}}
\end{quote}

This is why the letters \ta{ஓ} and \ta{உ} were taught on their own. A vowel at the \textbf{front} of a word cannot be a sign — there is nothing for it to sit on — so Tamil keeps a separate shape for exactly this job, and \ta{இன்று} is that shape doing it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{இ}} — then \textbf{\ta{ன்}} — then \textbf{\ta{று}}
  \item \emph{Point to:} the letter that could only ever be a free-standing one, and say why
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{இன்று}}, then \textbf{\ta{ஓடு}} — two words that open on a vowel
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{iṉṟu}, then say \emph{nēṟṟu}, then read \textbf{\ta{இன்று}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{இன்று}}. Why is the first shape a letter and not a sign? (Because the word \textbf{begins} with the vowel, so there is no consonant for a sign to sit on.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[muṉbu]{\ta{முன்பு} (muṉbu) — before, earlier}

\label{lesson:TA-C73-before}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: read \textbf{\ta{இன்று}}, and say what it means.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{முன்பு}}
\textbf{\ta{முன்பு}} (\emph{muṉbu}) — \textquotedblleft{}before, earlier\textquotedblright{}.

\textquotedblleft{}Before\textquotedblright{} — the general one, for anything earlier than the moment you are standing in.

You already have \ta{பிறகு} (\emph{piṟaku}), \textquotedblleft{}afterwards\textquotedblright{}. \ta{முன்பு} is its opposite, and between them the two put events in order without your needing a single verb tense to do it.

The \textbf{\ta{ன்}} in its middle is closed by a \ta{புள்ளி} and leans on the \ta{ப} after it — the same joint you read a moment ago inside \ta{இன்று}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Before and after, and a day on each side of today.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{muṉbu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{piṟaku}, then \emph{muṉbu} — the two directions in time
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nēṟṟu}, then \emph{muṉbu} — one is a day, one is any earlier moment
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nēṟṟu}, then read \textbf{\ta{இன்று}}, then say \emph{muṉbu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word is the opposite of \ta{பிறகு}? (\textbf{\ta{முன்பு}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mādam]{\ta{மாதம்} (mādam) — a month}

\label{lesson:TA-C73-month}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{muṉbu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மாதம்}}
\textbf{\ta{மாதம்}} (\emph{mādam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a month\textquotedblright{}.

A month.

You already know twelve of them by name — the Tamil months you met in their own chapter. This is the word for the unit itself, the one you need to say \textquotedblleft{}one month\textquotedblright{} rather than to name a particular one.

And another \textbf{\ta{ம்}} ending — like \ta{கோபம்}, \ta{பயம்} and \ta{பணம்} before it — on a word whose middle vowel is the long \textbf{\ta{ா}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Above the day: the month.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mādam}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nāḷ}, then \emph{mādam} — smaller, then bigger
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{இன்று}}, then say \emph{muṉbu}, then say \emph{mādam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மாதம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A month\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āṇḍu]{\ta{ஆண்டு} (āṇḍu) — a year}

\label{lesson:TA-C73-year}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mādam} mean, and what did \emph{muṉbu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{ஆண்டு}}
\textbf{\ta{ஆண்டு}} (\emph{āṇḍu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a year\textquotedblright{}.

A year — and it is the unit hiding inside a question you can already ask.

When you ask about someone's \ta{வயது} (\emph{vayathu}), their age, what is being counted is \ta{ஆண்டு}. The question was yours a long time ago; this is the word for what the answer is made of.

It opens on the free-standing \textbf{\ta{ஆ}}, because the word begins with that vowel — the same reason \ta{இன்று} opens on \ta{இ}. In the middle is the \textbf{\ta{ண்ட}} you first read in \ta{வண்டி}.

Three sizes now, each holding the one before it: \ta{நாள்}, \ta{மாதம்}, \ta{ஆண்டு}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: today, yesterday, and the three units above the day.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āṇḍu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vayathu}, then \emph{āṇḍu} — the question, and what the answer counts
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three sizes in order — \emph{nāḷ}, \emph{mādam}, \emph{āṇḍu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{muṉbu}, then say \emph{mādam}, then say \emph{āṇḍu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is counted when someone answers about their \ta{வயது}? (\textbf{\ta{ஆண்டு}} — years.)
\end{tcolorbox}
